1.summary: Spacing study sessions across days forces each retrieval to work harder, which strengthens long-term memory more than one long session.

options.A: A single pass the night before relies on cramming; the material fades quickly and cannot be revisited.
options.B: Short sessions spread over the four weeks create repeated retrieval with rest between them, the defining feature of spaced practice.
options.C: A single long rereading session is massed practice; familiarity rises but durable recall does not.
options.D: Highlighting is a passive activity and does not create the retrieval that spacing provides.

2.summary: Active recall means retrieving information from memory without looking at the material first.

options.A: Rereading feels productive but mostly builds familiarity, not retrieval strength.
options.B: Copying is transcription; the answer is on the page, so memory is not tested.
options.C: Producing the material from memory and then checking it is retrieval practice.
options.D: Listening is passive input; it does not require you to retrieve what you know.

3.summary: Retrieval practice and spaced repetition have strong evidence behind them; highlighting and all-nighters do not.

options.A: Self-testing is retrieval practice, one of the best-supported study techniques.
options.B: Highlighting is passive and can create an illusion of learning.
options.C: Spacing reviews over time improves retention.
options.D: An all-nighter harms sleep and consolidation and is not a study strategy to rely on.

4.summary: Interleaving means mixing different types or topics within one practice session.

options.A: Cramming is concentrated last-minute study, not mixing problem types.
options.B: Mixing problem types forces you to choose the right method each time.
options.C: Chunking groups information into meaningful units; it is not mixing topics.
options.D: Priming is exposure that makes later learning easier; it does not describe mixed practice.

5.summary: Sleep, especially after study, supports memory consolidation; it does not replace revision.

options.A: Sleep helps consolidate existing learning; it is not a shortcut to learning new material.
options.B: During sleep the brain stabilises and integrates what you studied.
options.C: Sleep supports but cannot replace revision and practice.
options.D: Sleep can reduce stress, but no strategy guarantees freedom from anxiety.

6.summary: A standard Pomodoro cycle is 25 minutes of focused work followed by a 5-minute break.

options.A: The short, timed focus block with a brief break is the Pomodoro pattern.
options.B: This reverses the pattern; the work block is the longer part.
options.C: Working without breaks for 90 minutes ignores the technique's short focus cycles.
options.D: Switching every two minutes prevents any focused work.

7.summary: Repeated rereading, rising errors, and task switching are signs of fatigue; feeling refreshed is not.

options.A: Losing absorption is a clear sign that attention has dropped.
options.B: More errors usually mean fatigue or overload.
options.C: Feeling refreshed and focused means the break worked; it is not a reason to stop.
options.D: Constant switching suggests concentration has broken down.

8.summary: Past papers are most useful as a rehearsal under exam conditions followed by a careful error review.

options.A: Reading the mark scheme first removes the retrieval practice and makes the paper feel easier than it is.
options.B: Simulating the exam exposes timing and knowledge gaps, and reviewing errors fixes them.
options.C: Memorising answers does not transfer to new questions and hides weak understanding.
options.D: Avoiding hard questions removes exactly the practice you need.

9.summary: Attempting the problem before seeing the solution turns a worked example into retrieval practice.

options.A: Trying first, even unsuccessfully, prepares you to notice why the solution works.
options.B: Copying the solution is passive and skips the thinking step.
options.C: Reading twice builds familiarity, not the ability to solve it yourself.
options.D: Skipping the example loses a chance to learn the method before practising.

10.summary: Light review, practical preparation, and sleep help; learning a hard topic for the first time does not.

options.A: A short review of key points reinforces memory without exhausting you.
options.B: Starting a difficult topic for the first time the night before adds stress and rarely sticks.
options.C: Preparing materials and travel removes avoidable exam-day problems.
options.D: Seven to nine hours supports attention and consolidation.

11.summary: Leaving a difficult question and returning later protects time for questions you can answer.

options.A: Sunk cost on one question can cost marks elsewhere.
options.B: Secure easier marks first, then return with a clear mind and remaining time.
options.C: A guess can be sensible, but spending all remaining time checking one answer wastes opportunities.
options.D: Handing in early gives up marks you could still earn.

12.summary: Reviewing mistakes by topic shows which areas to practise next.

options.A: A total score says little about which topics need work.
options.B: Restarting the syllabus ignores the evidence from the mock.
options.C: Grouping errors by topic turns the mock into a targeted study plan.
options.D: Comparing scores does not identify or fix your gaps.
